record.paper_title: Cyber-Physical Attacks on UAS Networks–Challenges and Open Research Problems
record.original_question: How should vulnerability-analysis frameworks for unmanned aerial system (UAS) networks model the interactions among communications, computation, sensors, and physical airframe components so that UAS are not treated merely as ordinary mobile ad hoc networks or isolated subsystems, and so that vulnerabilities created by interactions among heterogeneous UAV subsystems can be identified?

evidence.quote: Integration of multiple subsystems not only aggregates their individual vulnerabilities, but may result in new ones that are rooted in the interactions between those subsystems. Hence, UAS present the research community with a novel interdisciplinary challenge.

UAVs are cyber-physical systems, meaning that their operations are reliant on the interaction between physical and computational elements of the system. Consequently, security of a UAV is dependent not only on the computation and communications elements and protocols, but also on the physical components of the system [3]. This heavy entanglement of traditionally independent components requires a thorough framework for analysis of security issues in UAVs to be inclusive of the entire airframe. One obstacle in developing such a framework is the variety of UAV architectures and capabilities which makes the design of a generic model difficult.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an unmanned aerial system (UAS) network in which each unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is a cyber-physical system composed of four interacting subsystem classes: (i) a communications subsystem (radio links, networking protocols, ground-station data links), (ii) a computation subsystem (flight controller software, autopilot logic, mission processors), (iii) a sensor subsystem (GPS, IMU, cameras, barometers, etc.), and (iv) a physical airframe subsystem (actuators, motors, control surfaces, power and structural components). A UAS network consists of multiple such heterogeneous UAVs together with ground control stations and inter-UAV links.

Develop a vulnerability-analysis framework for UAS networks satisfying all of the following requirements:

1. The framework must model UAS not as ordinary mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) and not as isolated independent subsystems, but as integrated cyber-physical systems whose security depends on the coupling of the four subsystem classes above.

2. The framework must explicitly represent the interactions and information/energy flows among the communications, computation, sensor, and physical airframe subsystems, including cross-subsystem dependencies (e.g., a sensor spoof propagating through computation into physical actuation).

3. The framework must enable systematic identification of vulnerabilities that arise solely from the interaction of two or more heterogeneous subsystems and that are not present in any subsystem analyzed in isolation.

4. The framework must be generic enough to accommodate the diversity of UAV architectures, capabilities, and mission profiles (fixed-wing vs. rotary-wing, autonomous vs. tele-operated, single UAV vs. swarm), while still yielding actionable, architecture-specific vulnerability assessments.

Provide such a framework — including its formal modeling primitives, composition rules for inter-subsystem interactions, and a vulnerability-identification procedure — and justify that it meets requirements 1–4.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad open research challenge rather than a precise mathematical problem with a definitive answer. Subsequent work on UAS/UAV cyber-physical security has proposed various partial frameworks (attack taxonomies, threat models, STRIDE/DREAD adaptations, control-theoretic CPS security models), but no single universally adopted framework satisfying all stated requirements has emerged. The problem is therefore best classified as still open.

status_evidence.title: Cyber-Physical Attacks on UAS Networks–Challenges and Open Research Problems
status_evidence.snippet: UAS present the research community with a novel interdisciplinary challenge.
status_evidence.claim: The original framing identifies the development of such a framework as an open research problem.
